extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers of early-19th-century literary letters/essays
extracted.subtask_description: Personal critical letters commenting on poetry, epitaphs, and poetic collections — i.e., informal literary criticism and advice about poetic practice and editorial choices. Focus is on evaluating poetic quality, editorial handling, and imaginative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs should express plain, thorough feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Good epitaphs go to the bottom and express plain feeling rather than turgid or merely ornamental language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb praises Wordsworth's continuation of the 'Essay on Epitaphs' as 'the only sensible thing' on the subject and values the translation of a 'turgid epitaph into the plain feeling under it.' Avoid glib, patent phrasings that decorate rather than convey genuine thought about death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glib, repetitious inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated or formulaic thoughts make epitaphs and inscriptions smug and superficial rather than sincere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb criticizes the Ditton-upon-Thames gravestones for diversifying strains so that 'the same thought never occurs twice' — meaning the result is contrived banality. Ensure inscriptions arise from real reflection, not from rote phrasing applied to every grave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match inscription/content to the subject (suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions must suit the person or circumstance; misplaced sententiae produce absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an epitaph for an infant bearing 'Honor thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the land' is inappropriate. Check that tone, moralizing, and references are age- and context-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve authentic, concrete details
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain truthful, concrete particulars in narrative or poetic detail rather than substituting bland or safe alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb objects to substitutions made 'for the friendly reader' (a 'shell' in place of a household implement) — 'The tub was a good honest tub in its place.' Do not expunge or sanitize concrete items that give life and credibility to a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alter or sacrifice material to appease critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should resist excising or changing lines merely to placate 'scoundrels' or malice in critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb commends Wordsworth for not having 'sacrificed a verse to those scoundrels.' Preserve the work's integrity; avoid self-censorship that reduces artistic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and distinctness of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should feel fresh, have a distinct voice, and (when appropriate) reflect their period in the author's development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb notes some poems 'speak of an earlier period' and values pieces that are recognizably 'alive' and not simply repetitions of an 'old tone.' Strive for lines that feel 'quite alive' rather than imitative or merely competent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance over florid diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegant or 'fine' words without substantive matter create an 'aching vacuum' and fail to satisfy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb's reading of Lord Thurlow produced admiration for words but a sense of emptiness. Ensure language serves thought and feeling, not only ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative scope should remain comprehensible and morally/affectively accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessively remote or alien imaginative systems can disturb or repel readers; powerful imagination must not unduly estrange its audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb admired KeHama's power but found its unfamiliar faith-systems and vast foreign machinery 'put out of the pale' of his sympathies. Balance imaginative daring with ways for readers to enter and feel with the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational tone can be a strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational manner in long poems can create intimacy and nobility of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb calls 'The Excursion' 'the noblest conversational poem' (a 'day in heaven'). For certain subjects, a discursive, conversational mode is effective and valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and consistent tone across a collection
rubrics_metrics.description: A group's poems should fit together tonally and thematically so collections feel unified rather than disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb observes many of Wordsworth's pieces are 'so much of a piece they might have been written in the same week' — sometimes praise for unity, sometimes a note on the perception of sameness. Aim for coherence while preserving variety where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct, memorable characterization in narrative works
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should register as distinct personalities rather than merely fine-sounding types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb critiques Landor for lacking 'distinct character as a character.' Ensure characters have recognizable, memorable traits and contribute concretely to the work's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial apparatus (preface/explanations) helps critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear preface or account of the author's aims—especially about imagination—assists readers' understanding and appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb values Wordsworth's Preface and 'the account of what you mean by imagination.' Consider including explanatory material to orient readers to your aims without replacing the work itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and presentation matter (MS vs. print)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts often read 'raw'; printed, edited presentation can 'dress' and improve reception of poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb confesses he cannot endure his works in MS: 'All things read raw to me in MS.' Invest in careful proofreading and typographical presentation to maximize the work's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative imagery and sensory detail transform common things
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete sensory images (church coolness, sunsets, mountain scenery) can produce deep transformative impressions in readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb repeatedly points to the power of precise, sensory description (the 'instantaneous coolness' of a country church; a 'gorgeous sunset') to fix feelings. Cultivate fresh, vivid images to make ordinary scenes resonant.
